source.title: Ancestor-to-Creole Transfer is Not a Walk in the Park
source.authors: Heather Lent; Emanuele Bugliarello; Anders Søgaard

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream NER at pretraining checkpoints with different target-language perplexity stages, a conceptual test of V6's relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance. It does not test parameter, token, or compute scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-lingual perplexity curves over training and WALS distances, but these do not measure power-law scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute. The downstream NER checkpoint comparison is the result relevant to V6.
record.test_reason: The study trains one small BERT size on a tiny Bible corpus and tracks zero-shot perplexity on unseen Creole languages over training. It never varies parameters, tokens or compute, and fits no scaling law. The NER checkpoint comparison tracks zero-shot perplexity on an unseen target language in an overfitting regime. That is neither held-out pretraining loss nor scale, so it does not bear on V6 as stated. Kaplan et al. is cited only to justify using small models. The relation is citation only, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors conclude three things. Ordinary ancestor-to-Creole zero-shot transfer fails, and Creole perplexity rises initially (R1 falsified). A late 'compression' drop in Creole perplexity appears only for Creoles, even with random source languages. This compression does not give better downstream NER or few-shot learning (R2 falsified). Pretrained mBERT outperformed all their checkpoints.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains small multilingual models on language sets and measures cross-lingual transfer and downstream NER; it does not conduct scaling-law fits or compute-allocation experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: In a small, overfit BERT model, the late drop in zero-shot perplexity on Nigerian Pidgin did not bring better downstream NER. Post-compression checkpoints scored consistently worse than early or maximum-perplexity checkpoints across 3 seeds. The same pattern held for few-shot perplexity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero-shot perplexity on an unseen target language, tracked over training in an overfitting regime, need not predict downstream task performance in that language.

record.peer_reviewed: First Workshop on Insights from Negative Results in NLP
record.problems: The relevant downstream comparison is for one small model and one task. NER results are shown in a figure without numerical values in the text; the study reports three random seeds but no uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: All; no variation in parameters, tokens or compute.
All; no scaling in other regimes.
All; no scale variation, and no relation between held-out pretraining loss and downstream performance.

record.verdict_notes: Off-topic for scaling laws. Kaplan et al. (2020) appears only as support for small models on small data. The reader's V6 link and 'challenges' label are removed: no scale or pretraining-loss relationship is measured, and the NER values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss from smaller to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens.
Effect of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream NER at selected pretraining stages for one Nigerian Pidgin model, not scaling across model sizes or a general predictive relationship across tasks and models.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices.

rows.check: Marked 'reversed' against V6, but V6 concerns downstream gains with scale or pretraining loss. This post-compression checkpoint comes from a heavily overfit model whose source-language validation perplexity rises. Its lower metric is zero-shot perplexity on an unseen language, so it cannot test V6.
